title: Public Shelf Spike Calls
prompt: Spike #427: how the public shelf is stored, proven, kept clean and taken down. Put the covenant gate on the sheet, with any other fork the ADRs don't settle.
context: Settled by ADR-0077 and not reopened here: the shelf lists single Dispatches, never groups or people; a group opts in by an entrenched rules Proposal; each level publishes by its own shelf line on the Dispatch's ballot; an entry holds the title, the text, the publishing levels' names and their open-door addresses; the shelf is pull only. This sheet decides who may publish, the covenant gate, where entries live, what stops forgery by people holding a group's key, how long an entry stays, and what the steward may do to entries. The draft amendment (spike427/amendment-0077.md) assumes each recommendation.

decisions.title: Who may publish
decisions.question: What stops one person founding empty groups to flood the shelf, or publishing under a name that looks like another group's?
decisions.summary: There's no global identity (ADR-0009), so a reader can check that a group's key signed an entry, but not that the group is real or more than one person. Something scarce has to stand between a free key and a reader's screen: a person's judgment, a device's computation, or other groups' trust. This decides which. The covenant gate (next) and storage (decision 3) both assume the answer here.

options.label: Steward's signed list
options.summary: The steward adds each level's shelf address by hand to a signed list, the roll, that every reader fetches. Readers show only the levels it lists.
pros: A flood or a look-alike needs a person's yes
In the pilot, the steward is you, adding only your own groups
The roll is opaque keys and name commitments, not a directory
cons: One person's judgment and time
The steward learns who asked to be added, and how to reach them
A stolen steward key could list a look-alike

options.label: Work per entry
options.summary: Anyone may publish if their device spends about 30 seconds computing a hash puzzle per entry. Readers check the work.
pros: No gatekeeper
Runs with no person deciding anything
cons: A phone pays the same toll as a rented GPU that's far faster
Does nothing about look-alike names
Readers still download every record in a flood

options.label: Open, capped per key
options.summary: No admission. Readers show each key's few newest entries and nothing more.
pros: Nothing to run
No one decides who speaks
cons: A new key costs nothing, so the cap stops no one
Floods and look-alikes reach every reader
Still needs a relay change to stop the flood itself

options.label: Listed levels vouch
options.summary: A level reaches readers once two levels already on the shelf vouch for it with their keys.
pros: No single gatekeeper after the first few levels
Growth follows real relationships (ADR-0001)
cons: Each vouch is a public edge between two groups: the coalition graph the threat model protects
Two colluding groups can vouch in a hundred more
Still needs a steward to seed the first levels

decisions.recommendation_reason: It's the only option that stops both the flood and the look-alike without a global identity. It costs almost nothing in the pilot, because the steward is you adding your own groups. ADR-0013 and ADR-0035 already give a steward the reach decisions, so this adds a duty, not a new authority.

values.steward-roll: Stopped: each needs a person's yes
values.proof-of-work: Slowed for phones, not for rented hardware
values.vouched: Stopped only until two groups collude

values.steward-roll: Checked by hand at admission, then fixed to the key
values.vouched: Only as careful as the vouchers

values.steward-roll: The roll lists no names; the steward learns who asked
values.proof-of-work: Nothing new learned, but a hostile writer can fill the shelf
values.open-capped: Nothing new learned, but a hostile writer can fill the shelf
values.vouched: Publishes who vouches for whom: a group-to-group graph

values.steward-roll: One person, acting in public; an election after ADR-0035's threshold
Yes: add a handful of your own groups
values.proof-of-work: Yes, but every publishing phone waits
values.vouched: Needs a steward to start it anyway

values.steward-roll: Small: the roll record, the reader's check, a steward script
values.proof-of-work: Small to medium: the puzzle and its tuning

values.steward-roll: You add each level and post the roll again every three weeks
values.proof-of-work: Battery and time on every publishing phone
Medium: the difficulty must keep pace with hardware
values.vouched: High: what a withdrawn vouch does to entries

values.steward-roll: High: the roll can later list everyone or no one, with no change to records
values.open-capped: Hard to tighten once groups expect to publish freely
values.vouched: Low: published vouches can't be unpublished

risks.risk: The steward's key is stolen and used to list a look-alike under a group's name
risks.mitigation: Keep the key on your own computer, never on the relay. Every roll change is public. A level's devices warn their members when another key holds their name. Replace the key by an app release.

risks.risk: The steward becomes a bottleneck or a gatekeeper
risks.mitigation: Public reason codes, and ADR-0035's election threshold moves the seat. The roll fails closed after 30 days, so an absent steward can't leave a stale list up.

risks.risk: A sock-puppet group gets admitted
risks.mitigation: The pilot admits only your own groups. After it, the admission checks the covenant gate requires apply.

risks.risk: A flood reaches every reader's phone
risks.mitigation: None within the option

risks.risk: Vouches publish a map of which groups trust which
risks.mitigation: None within the option

examples.title: Mastodon Server Covenant
examples.detail: joinmastodon.org lists only servers whose admins commit to its moderation rules. A server that won't commit still runs; it just isn't listed. That's reach, not existence, as in ADR-0013.

examples.title: Usenet moderated newsgroups
examples.detail: A moderated group's posts reach readers only after its moderator approves them. Anyone can still start an unmoderated group.

examples.title: Twitter Blue's paid checkmarks (November 2022)
examples.detail: Once anyone could buy verification, an account posing as Eli Lilly announced that insulin was free, and the company's stock fell. A name check that costs nothing stops nothing.

examples.title: Hashcash and Nostr NIP-13
examples.detail: Proof of work per message, with tunable difficulty (Adam Back, 1997; Nostr's NIP-13). Senders with better hardware pay far less than phones.

examples.title: The PGP web of trust
examples.detail: Keys vouched for by other keys. It never reached ordinary users, and it publishes who signed whose key.

decisions.title: The covenant gate
decisions.question: Does publishing wait for the worded covenant, or may a pilot limited to your own groups go first?
decisions.summary: ADR-0035 says the eternal core must be worded, and read by counsel, before discovery or reach enforcement ships. ADR-0077 made shelf publishing wait on it. Before groups outside your circle publish, five things must be written: the eternal core; the shelf clause a group agrees to when it turns the shelf on; the steward's rules (who holds the seat, what they may do, that every act is public, how to appeal); the admission checks; and counsel's answers on hosting public text, such as whether a DMCA agent is needed. This decides whether a pilot where the roll lists only levels you belong to may publish first. It assumes the steward's list from decision 1.

options.label: Your groups first
options.summary: Publishing ships now, but the steward adds only levels you belong to. Outside groups wait on the five items and the outside review (ADR-0058).
pros: Tests the whole loop with real, consenting groups
No reach decisions about strangers before the rules exist
Lifting the limit is a roll change, not a rebuild
cons: You're member and steward at once
Pilot groups' names go public, by their own entrenched vote
The wording can keep slipping while the pilot runs

options.label: Wait for the wording
options.summary: No group publishes until all five items are written and read. The opt-in and the ballot line (#430) can still merge.
pros: Nothing goes public under a group's name before the rules exist
Matches ADR-0035 as written
cons: The shelf, Ask to join from it, and Bedfellows go untested in the pilot
Delays the epic's success criteria
The wording session isn't scheduled yet

options.label: Interim covenant
options.summary: Ship the placeholder line as a provisional, non-eternal shelf rule, and admit outside groups by hand now.
pros: Real outside groups in the pilot
Gives the steward a written rule to apply
cons: People will treat a provisional rule as the real one
You judge strangers' words with no appeal rules and no counsel
Brings forward the outside review, due before outside groups use the app

decisions.recommendation_reason: It's the only option that runs the shelf for real while no stranger's group gains reach under rules that don't exist yet. It's reversible with a roll change, and lifting it can share #435's trigger: before any group outside your circle, or before the outside review.

values.own-groups-first: Only groups you're in, by their own entrenched vote

values.interim-covenant: Yes, by one person under a placeholder

values.own-groups-first: The full loop with real groups
A few consenting groups' names are public; a hostile reader learns little
values.interim-covenant: A hostile group could publish under an untested provisional rule

values.own-groups-first: You hold the roll and vote in every group on it
Same code as the full shelf, plus a line of copy
Add your own groups; post the roll again every three weeks
values.interim-covenant: Judge every outside request and appeal
Medium: a provisional rule to retire later

values.own-groups-first: High: drop a level from the roll
values.interim-covenant: Low: outside groups' expectations, and the precedent of a provisional rule

risks.risk: Being steward of groups you vote in looks like control
risks.mitigation: Every roll change is public with a reason code, and the pilot notice says so. The seat converts by ADR-0035's threshold.

risks.risk: The wording keeps slipping, and the pilot limit becomes permanent
risks.mitigation: Name the trigger: lift the limit only with the five items done and the outside review booked.

risks.risk: Counsel finds a hosting duty, such as a DMCA agent, after outside text is already up
risks.mitigation: Ask counsel before lifting the gate

risks.risk: A vulnerable group turns the shelf on without understanding it
risks.mitigation: The opt-in sits only in Rules, at the entrenched bar, with a plain line on what it exposes (#430)

examples.title: Bluesky's invite-only beta
examples.detail: The network stayed invite-only through 2023 while its moderation tools and policies were built, and opened to everyone in February 2024.

examples.title: Mastodon Server Covenant
examples.detail: Listing on joinmastodon.org comes with written commitments a server makes before it's listed. Reach waits on the rules.

examples.title: Gmail's invite-only years (2004–2007)
examples.detail: Access was staged by invitation while the service grew, and opened fully only later.

examples.title: #366 and #435 in this repo
examples.detail: You accepted a closed door's gaps for the pilot inside your circle, and set a trigger to harden it before outside groups or the outside review.

decisions.title: Where entries live
decisions.question: Does the relay change to hold the shelf, and how much does it get to know?
decisions.summary: Shelf entries are the first bytes the relay holds that anyone may read. Today a mailbox id is both the right to read and the right to write, so a mailbox everyone reads is one anyone can fill. This decides how the relay stops that, and how much it knows. It assumes the steward's list from decision 1; with an open shelf, only the checked shelf works.

options.label: Public mailboxes
options.summary: Two routes and a DELETE. The relay stores a record under the hash of a write key and serves reads by that hash. Each listed level has one mailbox, and the roll has one.
pros: The relay checks a hash and counts bytes, nothing else
Strangers can't put a byte in front of a reader
Small: no new table and no signature check; #435 can reuse it
cons: Readers make one request per listed level
The shelf's rules live in every reader
Anyone holding a level's key can fill that level's 512 KiB

options.label: One checked shelf
options.summary: New /v1/shelf routes. The relay checks each record's signature against the steward's roll, caps each level and keeps key retirements. Readers make one request.
pros: One request reads everything
The relay refuses retired and unlisted keys
Per-level caps at the relay
cons: The relay parses public records and holds the steward's key: policy at the relay
Ties the relay's operator to the steward
About three times the code on the security-critical service

options.label: Ordinary mailbox
options.summary: No relay change in the pilot: a well-known weekly mailbox for entries, another for the roll, and readers filter. Public mailboxes come later, on a trigger.
pros: No relay work now
The relay stays exactly as it is
cons: Anyone who reads the app's code can fill the week's 64 MiB, and every reader's phone downloads it
No DELETE, so a takedown only hides the entry
A migration later

decisions.recommendation_reason: The relay stays blind to what it holds: it hashes a key and counts bytes. Strangers still can't fill the shelf's well-known mailboxes. No door link has that exposure, because the shelf's ids go out to everyone. It's the smallest relay change that does this, and the same routes could close #435's gap.

values.write-keys: A hash and byte counts; it never parses a record
values.signed-shelf: Parses records, checks signatures, holds the steward's key

values.write-keys: One request per listed level, plus the roll; well under 1 MiB at pilot size
values.plain-mailbox: Five weeks of mailboxes, up to 320 MiB under attack
No: hidden only, until it expires

values.write-keys: Private data as today; a posting device's address is tied to the level live
values.signed-shelf: The same, and the relay becomes a policy point that whoever seizes it could repurpose
values.plain-mailbox: Private data as today; the shelf is easy to blank

values.write-keys: Small: two routes and a DELETE, reusing the blob code
values.signed-shelf: Medium to large: tables, framing, Ed25519, the roll

values.write-keys: Low on the relay, moderate in readers
High: the routes can go, and the records describe themselves
values.signed-shelf: Medium: state held at the relay to migrate
values.plain-mailbox: Medium: readers and records change when the routes arrive

risks.risk: Someone holding a level's key fills that level's mailbox, so its new entries are refused, or deletes its entries
risks.mitigation: Capped at 512 KiB; members' devices delete forgeries; the key changes at a membership end

risks.risk: Readers' requests grow with the number of listed levels
risks.mitigation: Revisit at 100 listed levels; paged reads can stay the same for every reader

risks.risk: Whoever holds the relay's server can change the shelf's policy
risks.mitigation: Readers check signatures and the roll anyway

risks.risk: One stranger blanks the shelf every week
risks.mitigation: Accept for the pilot, and build public mailboxes before outside groups publish

risks.risk: A malicious relay withholds records or ignores a DELETE
risks.mitigation: Accepted: the relay is trusted for order and time (ADR-0073), and the outside review covers it

examples.title: Tahoe-LAFS mutable files
examples.detail: Separate write and read capabilities. A storage server accepts a change only from whoever holds the write-enabler secret.

examples.title: Freenet's signed subspace keys
examples.detail: Anyone can fetch content by its public key, and only the private key's holder can insert under it.

examples.title: Nostr relays (NIP-01)
examples.detail: Relays store signed events and check their signatures. Paid relays restrict who may write.

examples.title: The Update Framework (TUF)
examples.detail: Signed metadata under a root key shipped in the client, which expires so that a stale copy fails closed. The roll follows the same model.

decisions.title: Forgery by key holders
decisions.question: What stops a member, or someone who has left, from signing under the group's name?
decisions.summary: A reader can verify only that someone holding a level's shelf key signed, and no option in decision 1 changes that. Every member holds the key, and someone who leaves keeps whatever they could read, as with a front door's key (#288). Whatever you pick here, readers wait a day before showing a new record, and members' devices delete any record their own fold didn't make. So a forgery shows only if nobody in the level opens the app within that day. This decides what happens to the key when a membership ends.

options.label: New key per group key
options.summary: The shelf key comes from the group's current secret, so the key change after a leave or removal (#98) retires it automatically. The steward then adds the new address.
pros: Someone who left can't sign once the key changes
No new event and no vote
For your own groups, your device can read the new address itself
cons: New entries pause until the steward adds the new address
Shows readers that the group's membership changed, and roughly when
A coalition's key still never changes (ADR-0074)

options.label: Fresh key by vote
options.summary: When a membership ends, the key retires. A member proposes a fresh one at the ordinary bar (3 to 14 days; ADR-0075 §5), and the steward adds it.
pros: The group decides when it's back
The same cut-off for someone who left
cons: A pause of days after every leave
A new kind of Proposal
The same public signal

options.label: Keep one key
options.summary: One key for as long as the opt-in is on. Rely on the day's wait and members' devices deleting forgeries.
pros: No pause and no signal
Nothing for the steward to do
cons: Anyone who was ever a member can forge for as long as the shelf is on
In a quiet group, each forgery is a window for a smear
Even a removal (ADR-0016) doesn't end it

decisions.recommendation_reason: It cuts off someone who left at the moment the group already changes its key, with no new event or vote, and it matches your choice for doors (#288). The pause and the steward's re-add are small in a pilot of a few groups, and your device handles them for your own.

values.epoch-key: Ends at the key change, minutes to hours later
The day's wait, then members' devices delete it
values.ordinary-vote: The day's wait, then members' devices delete it
values.keep-key: The day's wait, then members' devices delete it

values.epoch-key: Until the steward adds the new address; the same day for your groups
A retire record and a new address show that the membership changed
values.ordinary-vote: The same, plus when the vote ran
values.keep-key: No signal, but a removed hostile member keeps the group's public voice

values.epoch-key: Small: derive the key from the current secret, and post a retire at the key change
values.ordinary-vote: Medium: a new rules value and Proposal
The steward's re-adds, plus the group's votes

values.epoch-key: High: moving to one kept key later is a change in how it's derived
values.keep-key: Low, once someone who left has forged

risks.risk: A member who knows a removal vote is coming forges during its 14 days
risks.mitigation: They're still a member then, so the day's wait and members' devices' checks apply, and the key changes at the removal

risks.risk: A quiet group, where nobody opens the app for a day, shows a forgery
risks.mitigation: The ballot line and Rules say the group's devices check its shelf entries only when someone opens the app

risks.risk: The membership signal tells a hostile reader that a group lost someone
risks.mitigation: It shows when, never who, and only for groups on the shelf

examples.title: HMV's Twitter account (January 2013)
examples.detail: Staff being laid off live-tweeted the firings from the company's shared login. A shared credential outlives its holders' place in the group.

examples.title: Changing shared secrets when someone leaves
examples.detail: Standard offboarding, and this project already does it for group keys (#98) and front doors (#288).

examples.title: Wikipedia's pending changes
examples.detail: On protected articles, edits by new accounts wait for review before readers see them. The day's wait has the same shape.

decisions.title: How long an entry stays
decisions.question: How long does a published Dispatch stay on the shelf?
decisions.summary: A longer life helps newcomers find a group's words. It also builds a fuller record of what each group said, for any hostile reader and for whoever seizes the relay. Under every option, a reader shows at most each level's 10 newest entries, and a takedown still works at once. This decides the default life, and whether devices post entries again to keep them up.

options.label: 30 days
options.summary: 30 days from the level's pass: the relay's own blob retention. Nothing posts it again, so a group publishes again to stay findable.
pros: The relay holds at most a month
Matches ADR-0057 and the relay's 30-day limit, so nothing posts again
Old words don't keep standing for a group that has moved on
cons: A quiet group drops off the shelf
Ask to join from an entry lasts only a month

options.label: 90 days
options.summary: Members' devices post each entry again every three weeks, until 90 days after the pass.
pros: Newcomers find more
cons: Three times what a scraper or a seizure gets at once
Each repeat post ties a device's address to the group again, live
Needs a refresh duty in every level

options.label: Until taken down
options.summary: Devices keep posting it again until the level takes it down or turns the shelf off.
pros: A group's public words stay until it decides otherwise
cons: The shelf becomes a standing record of every group's words: a list by ideology
Grows without end, until the caps start dropping entries
Devices post again forever

decisions.recommendation_reason: It's the life the relay already gives every blob, so there's no refresh duty and no extra posts that tie a device's address to a group. It keeps the shelf a stream of recent words rather than an archive of who said what.

values.30-days: A month of words at a time
A group publishes about monthly to stay findable

tradeoffs.dimension: Posts that tie an address to a group

values.until-down: More posts, and storage that keeps growing

values.30-days: High: the life can be lengthened later
values.90-days: Medium: shortening it drops entries groups expect to see
values.until-down: Low: an archive once kept is kept elsewhere too

risks.risk: Groups feel pushed to publish monthly to stay visible: pressure toward engagement
risks.mitigation: No counts and no ranking (DESIGN.md), and Discover says plainly that entries last 30 days

risks.risk: A scraper archives everything anyway
risks.mitigation: Nothing technical stops it. The ballot line says entries can be copied.

risks.risk: A group's old words go on standing for it after its views change
risks.mitigation: Takedown by vote, or a shorter life

examples.title: Craigslist listings
examples.detail: A listing expires after 7, 30 or 45 days, depending on its category, and must be posted again to stay up.

examples.title: Nostr NIP-40
examples.detail: An event can carry an expiration time, after which relays drop it.

examples.title: Instagram and Snapchat Stories
examples.detail: Posts that vanish after 24 hours: a deliberate choice to keep what someone said from becoming a permanent record.

examples.title: Mastodon's automatic post deletion
examples.detail: Since version 3.5, a person can have their posts deleted once they pass an age they choose.

decisions.title: A level that breaks the covenant
decisions.question: When the steward finds an entry that breaks the covenant, what leaves the shelf, and when?
decisions.summary: ADR-0077 left open whether a suspended group's entries leave at once or by vote. ADR-0013 says breaking the covenant costs reach and that a group can appeal by vote, but Reconcile-the-group, which would hold that vote, is deferred (ADR-0074). Two things hold whatever you pick: a member's suspension inside a group (ADR-0016) changes nothing on the shelf, and a group takes its own entries down by its own ordinary vote. This decides what power the steward has over entries already published.

options.label: Entry at once
options.summary: The steward withholds one entry at once, with a public reason, and suspends a level's key only for a severe or repeated breach. Either stands until lifted, or until the entry ages out.
pros: Harm is gone from every reader's next read
Touches only what broke the rule
Public reason codes
cons: One person's judgment in the pilot
Appeals go to that same person, by hand
The bytes stay on the relay until they expire

options.label: Level, then confirm
options.summary: The steward suspends the level's key at once. The suspension lapses after 7 days unless the steward confirms it publicly, as in ADR-0016.
pros: The familiar suspend-then-decide shape
Forces a second look
cons: Removes all of a group's entries over one
With no Reconcile-the-group yet, the same person confirms
A lapse can bring harmful words back

options.label: Only the group's vote
options.summary: The steward can refuse to add or re-add a level, but never hides what's already up. Entries leave by the level's own vote, by age, or when it turns the shelf off.
pros: No editorial power over words already published
Simple
cons: Harmful words stay up for as long as 30 days
Dropping the whole level is the steward's only tool, and a blunter one

decisions.recommendation_reason: It takes a harmful entry off every reader's next read and leaves the group's other words alone, and every act is public on the roll. In a pilot of your own groups it will rarely be needed. The appeal by vote arrives with the covenant gate.

values.group-vote-only: Nothing, or the whole level if it's dropped

values.entry-first: One person, acting in public, with reason codes
Withholding is public, so readers see that a group was judged
values.level-lapse: The same, for the whole group

values.entry-first: By hand to the steward; by vote once Reconcile-the-group exists
Small: the roll's lists and the reader's check
High: lift it on the roll

risks.risk: The steward withholds words they disagree with
risks.mitigation: Public reason codes, the level's appeal, and the seat converting to an election (ADR-0035)

risks.risk: A legal demand needs the bytes gone, not just hidden
risks.mitigation: The operator deletes the row by hand and the roll notes it as legal. Counsel's question is part of the covenant gate.

risks.risk: A withheld entry stays readable on the relay itself
risks.mitigation: For at most 30 days; the operator can delete it on a legal demand

examples.title: Bluesky's labelers
examples.detail: Moderation services publish signed labels that clients honour to hide a post or warn about it, without deleting it from the network. The roll's withheld list works the same way.

examples.title: Certificate revocation lists (RFC 5280)
examples.detail: An issuer publishes a signed list of revoked certificates, and clients check it before trusting one.

examples.title: Mastodon moderation
examples.detail: A server's admins can remove a single post or suspend an account, and many servers publish their moderation decisions.

examples.title: DMCA notice and takedown (17 U.S.C. §512)
examples.detail: A host that takes material down on notice keeps its safe harbor, and registers a designated agent with the Copyright Office.
